content.title: Slope, Intercepts, and Linear Equations
content.overview: This lesson covers the fundamental components of linear relationships: slope (m), the x-intercept, and the y-intercept (b). You will learn to convert intercepts into coordinate points, calculate slope between two points, and construct the slope-intercept equation (y = mx + b).
learning_objectives: Convert x-intercepts and y-intercepts into coordinate points.
Calculate the slope (m) of a line using two points.
Determine the equation of a line in slope-intercept form (y = mx + b) given a point and an intercept.

sections.title: Understanding Intercepts as Points
sections.content: An intercept is the point where a line crosses an axis. To use them in calculations, you must express them as coordinates. An x-intercept of 'a' means the line passes through the point (a, 0). A y-intercept of 'b' means the line passes through the point (0, b). Recognizing that the 'other' coordinate is always zero is the first step in solving linear relationship problems.

sections.title: Calculating Slope (m)
sections.content: Slope represents the 'rise over run' or the rate of change between two points (x1, y1) and (x2, y2). The formula is m = (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1). The order of points does not matter as long as you are consistent in the numerator and denominator. A positive slope rises from left to right, while a negative slope falls.

sections.title: Building the Equation: y = mx + b
sections.content:
The slope-intercept form is the most common way to express a linear equation. In this form, 'm' is the slope and 'b' is the y-coordinate of the y-intercept. If you have the slope and any point (x, y), you can solve for 'b' by plugging the values into the equation and isolating the variable.

![A flowchart showing the steps: Identify Intercepts as Points, Calculate Slope m, Solve for b in y=mx+b, and Verify with Point.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/34fc41e3-b1f9-48f3-a378-a7adae349508-1786505621092-777.webp)

worked_examples.question: A line passes through the point (2, 3) and has an x-intercept of 5. Find the equation of the line.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Convert the x-intercept to a point. An x-intercept of 5 is the point (5, 0). Step 2: Calculate the slope (m) using (2, 3) and (5, 0). m = (0 - 3) / (5 - 2) = -3 / 3 = -1. Step 3: Use y = mx + b to find b. Plug in m = -1 and the point (2, 3): 3 = (-1)(2) + b. Step 4: Solve for b. 3 = -2 + b, so b = 5. Step 5: Write the final equation: y = -x + 5.

common_mistakes: Swapping the x and y coordinates when writing intercepts (e.g., writing an x-intercept of 5 as (0, 5) instead of (5, 0)).
Subtracting coordinates in the wrong order in the slope formula (e.g., (y2 - y1) / (x1 - x2)).
Forgetting to change the sign of 'b' when moving terms across the equals sign.
exam_tips: Always verify your final equation by plugging the original point back into it. If the equation is correct, the point will satisfy it.
If a question asks for the y-intercept, look at the 'b' value in y = mx + b immediately.
Watch for vertical lines (undefined slope, x = constant) and horizontal lines (zero slope, y = constant).
content.recap: To find a linear equation, identify two points (converting intercepts if necessary), calculate the slope (m), solve for the y-intercept (b) using y = mx + b, and verify your result with a known point.

knowledge_claims.content: An x-intercept of 'a' is represented by the coordinate point (a, 0).
A y-intercept of 'b' is represented by the coordinate point (0, b).
The slope formula is m = (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1).
In the equation y = mx + b, the variable 'm' represents the slope of the line.
In the equation y = mx + b, the variable 'b' represents the y-coordinate of the y-intercept.
To find the y-intercept 'b' when you have the slope and a point, substitute the slope and the point's coordinates into y = mx + b and solve for b.
A linear equation can be verified by substituting a known point (x, y) into the equation to see if the equality holds true.
A common error is reversing the slope formula to (x2 - x1) / (y2 - y1); the change in y must always be in the numerator.
A line with a negative slope will decrease (go down) as it moves from left to right on a graph.
A line with a positive slope will increase (go up) as it moves from left to right on a graph.
If a line has an x-intercept of 5 and a y-intercept of 5, its slope is -1.
The slope of a horizontal line is 0, and its equation takes the form y = b.
